blueprint_topic: Management of Care — early interdisciplinary palliative-care referral concurrent with active oncology treatment
stem: A client with advanced cancer receiving active antineoplastic treatment has persistent pain, nausea, and anxiety. The client says, 'I thought palliative care was only for when cancer treatment stops.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Palliative care can be added during cancer treatment to address pain, nausea, anxiety, and quality-of-life goals without requiring antineoplastic therapy to stop.
options.B: Palliative care is generally deferred until disease-directed options are exhausted, because symptom management during active therapy remains part of routine oncology care.
options.C: Palliative care may be used during active treatment for physical symptoms, but emotional support and goals-of-care work are usually reserved for a later hospice transition.
options.D: Referral to palliative care signals a shift away from disease-directed treatment, so the oncology plan should be changed before the palliative team becomes involved.

rationale: A is correct. ASCO's 2024 guideline recommends early specialist interdisciplinary palliative care for patients with advanced cancer alongside active cancer treatment, with particular attention to uncontrolled symptoms and quality-of-life concerns. NCI states that palliative care may be provided at any point during cancer care and that cancer treatment may continue while palliative care is received. NCI also identifies pain, nausea, anxiety, emotional concerns, and goals-of-care discussions as appropriate palliative-care needs. B is incorrect because palliative care is not deferred until disease-directed treatment is exhausted. C is incorrect because palliative care addresses emotional and psychosocial needs and goals of care during the cancer trajectory, not merely after transition toward hospice. D is incorrect because referral to palliative care does not itself signal discontinuation of disease-directed treatment or require a treatment-goal change before referral.
educational_objective: Explain that clients with advanced cancer can receive interdisciplinary palliative care early and concurrently with active antineoplastic treatment to address physical symptoms, psychosocial distress, and quality-of-life goals without requiring a transition to hospice.
source_organization: American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO); National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Palliative Care for Patients With Cancer: ASCO Guideline Update; Palliative Care in Cancer
source_version_date: ASCO guideline published online May 15, 2024 and in print July 1, 2024; NCI fact sheet reviewed November 1, 2021; sources rechecked 2026-08-20
source_locator: ASCO 2024 guideline — Recommendations: patients with advanced solid tumors and hematologic malignancies should be referred to specialized interdisciplinary palliative-care teams early in the disease course alongside active cancer treatment; dedicated specialist palliative care is recommended for unaddressed physical, psychosocial, or spiritual distress, and early involvement is emphasized for uncontrolled symptoms/QOL concerns. ASCO explanatory text following the recommendations clarifies that 'early' means not waiting for cessation of antineoplastic-directed therapy. NCI 'Palliative Care in Cancer' — 'What is palliative care?', 'What issues are addressed in palliative care?', 'When is palliative care used in cancer care?', and 'What is the difference between palliative care and hospice?': palliative care addresses symptoms including pain/nausea and emotional concerns including anxiety, may begin at any point, and may occur while cancer treatment continues.
source_claim_supported: Current ASCO guidance supports early interdisciplinary palliative-care referral alongside active cancer treatment for advanced cancer, especially with uncontrolled symptoms or QOL concerns. NCI directly supports concurrent cancer treatment and palliative care and identifies pain, nausea, anxiety, psychosocial concerns, and goals-of-care communication as palliative-care domains. These sources also distinguish palliative care from hospice.
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care, PDF file page index 10 / printed page 7: identify/collaborate with multidisciplinary team members, assess the need for referrals and obtain necessary orders, initiate/evaluate/update the plan of care, and utilize resources to promote quality client care. Detailed Management of Care content also includes a Referrals section on assessing referral needs for existing or potential problems.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the original absolute-word distractor pattern ('only', 'entirely', 'all', 'must'). The final alternatives are length-balanced and test realistic misconceptions about timing, scope of palliative services, and confusion between palliative care and hospice while preserving one source-supported best answer.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly reflects ASCO early concurrent palliative-care guidance and NCI's statement that cancer treatment may continue while palliative care addresses physical and psychosocial needs.
option_audit.B: Plausible wait-until-treatment-exhausted misconception; incorrect because ASCO recommends early palliative involvement alongside active treatment rather than deferral until disease-directed options are exhausted.
option_audit.C: Plausible symptom-only misconception; incorrect because NCI includes emotional concerns and goals-of-care communication within palliative care during the cancer trajectory.
option_audit.D: Plausible palliative-equals-hospice misconception; incorrect because palliative referral can coexist with disease-directed treatment and does not itself require a change to hospice goals.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type distractor absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are closely balanced (A 162, B 171, C 172, D 165 characters); the correct option is not the longest.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are parallel explanations of when palliative care is appropriate and how it relates to active oncology treatment.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified in the pre-stage audit; B, C, and D each contain a distinct restriction contradicted by ASCO/NCI guidance. Post-fetch adversarial reread is still required.
